description: Our Earth is constantly changing. From rising temperatures and shifting precipitation patterns to changes in vegetation and oceans, these variations reveal important signals about our planet. But how can we distinguish natural fluctuations from significant long-term trends? By using NASA's Earth observation data, we aim to uncover meaningful patterns, visualize changes, and make Earth system science more accessible to everyone.
summary:
UrHeatixel is an interactive mapping website designed to monitor the spatial expansion of areas with high land surface temperatures (LST) across Hanoi and identify locations requiring priority intervention. The project integrates three data sources: land surface temperature from NASA MODIS (MOD11A1), vegetation index (NDVI) from NASA MODIS (MOD13A2), and built-up land cover data from Esri Sentinel-2 Land Cover. The data are analyzed at the pixel level for two time points: 2017 and 2025.

The results reveal that high-temperature areas increased from 21.1% to 65.8% of the total study area, gradually spreading from the urban core toward the outskirts. Over the same period, built-up areas expanded by 265 km², while vegetation cover declined. By overlaying temperature and vegetation data, the project identified 192 km² of hotspots, including 48.9 km² classified as critically urgent, concentrated across 23 wards and communes.

This project is particularly important because the urban heat island effect directly affects the health, energy consumption, and quality of life of nearly 9 million residents in Hanoi. UrHeatixel transforms satellite data into clear, accessible, and visual evidence, helping urban planners and policymakers identify where green spaces and urban cooling interventions should be prioritized.
details:
UrHeatixel

Monitoring the spatial dynamics of high land surface temperature zones to identify urban expansion trends in Hanoi

1. Project overview

- UrHeatixel uses satellite data to monitor how the high land surface temperature zones of Hanoi have spread over the period 2017 – 2025, why they have spread, and where intervention is needed first. The project takes part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Hanoi and is carried out by the team Long Geo – Geomatics.

- Context. Urbanization replaces farmland, water bodies and trees with concrete, roofs and roads. These surfaces absorb and retain more heat, creating the urban heat island effect: urban areas are hotter than their surroundings. Urban heat islands affect public health, cooling energy demand and residents' quality of life. Hanoi is urbanizing rapidly, yet there is no visual tool showing how far the hot zones are spreading.

- Idea. Analyze satellite imagery pixel by pixel and combine three layers of information:

a.     Land surface temperature (LST) from NASA MODIS, showing where it is hot.

b.     Built-up area from Esri Sentinel-2 Land Cover, showing where the city is expanding.

c.     Vegetation index (NDVI) from NASA MODIS, showing whether green cover remains or is lost.

- Overlaying these layers makes it possible to identify hotspots: places that are both very hot and lacking green cover, which should be prioritized for intervention.

- Product: A public, free, interactive map website: UrHeatixel. The website tells the story in 5 parts following the flow Current state → Trend → Cause (built-up area) → Cause (vegetation) → Action. Wherever the user hovers the mouse, the website shows the pixel value and the name of the commune/ward at that location.

2. Objectives and research questions

- The overall objective is to identify urban expansion trends through the dynamics of high land surface temperature zones, and to determine the areas in Hanoi that should be prioritized for intervention. The project answers 5 questions, each corresponding to one part of the website:

05 · Action

- Specific objectives:

+ Build map layers of land surface temperature, built-up land and vegetation for two time points, 2017 and 2025.

+ Quantify the area and changes of each layer by class.

+ Identify hotspots down to each 1 km cell and each commune/ward.

+ Publish the results on an interactive website that anyone can use.

3. Study area

- The study area is the whole of Hanoi city within its new 2025 administrative boundaries, comprising 126 communes/wards after the reorganization of administrative units.

- Location: approximately 105.28°E – 106.02°E and 20.56°N – 21.39°N, bordering Bắc Ninh, Hưng Yên, Ninh Bình and Phú Thọ.

- Area: approximately 3,356 km² (calculated from the 10 m land cover layer). On the 1 km MODIS grid, the area is covered by 4,509 pixels, equivalent to 3,614.5 km² (slightly larger because the edge pixels extend beyond the boundary).

- Characteristics: a dense urban core in the center and along both banks of the Red River; the western and northern outskirts are mainly farmland, forest and mountainous areas (Ba Vì).

- Time: two time points, 2017 and 2025, 8 years apart.

4. Data sources

- Notes on the data:

+ LST: raw values are multiplied by a scale factor of 0.02 to obtain Kelvin, then 273.15 is subtracted to obtain °C. On cloudy days, pixels have no value, so many days must be combined into an annual mean image.

+ LULC: only the Built Area class (built-up land) is used; each 10 m pixel corresponds to 0.0001 km².

+ NDVI: values range from −1 to 1; the higher the value, the more green vegetation; values near 0 or negative usually indicate water or surfaces without vegetation.

The results are presented following the 5 parts of the website. The area of the 1 km layers is calculated from 4,509 pixels with latitude correction (total 3,614.5 km²); the area of built-up land is calculated from 10 m pixels (total 3,356.26 km²).

- The annual mean LST in 2025 is about 3.6 °C lower than in 2017, mainly due to differences in weather and in the number of cloudy days between the two years. Therefore, °C values are not compared directly between the two years; instead, the data are normalized in the next step.

5.2 Trend of high-temperature zones (Part 02)

- The high-temperature zone (High + Very High) expanded from 761.6 km² (21.07%) in 2017 to 2,377.1 km² (65.77%) in 2025. LST was min–max normalized to 0–1 within each year, then divided into 5 classes with a step of 0.2 (Very Low, Low, Moderate, High, Very High).

- Class change. The change code of each pixel = 2017 class × 10 + 2025 class.

+ Class increase: 2,106.7 km² (58.28%). The largest is Moderate → High (code 34): 1,572.2 km² (43.50%).

+ Unchanged class: 1,420.4 km² (39.30%).

+ Class decrease: only 87.4 km² (2.42%).

- Direction of spread. The high-temperature zone has shifted away from the center: its mean distance to Hoàn Kiếm Lake increased from 20.0 km to 26.8 km, and the share lying within a 10 km radius decreased from 18.8% to 9.4%. This shows that the high-temperature zone is spreading from the urban core to the periphery.

5.5 LST – NDVI relationship and hotspots for intervention (Part 05)

Places with less green cover are getting hotter: the correlation between normalized LST and NDVI is r = −0.24 in 2017 and r = −0.42 in 2025. On the original data, an NDVI increase of 0.1 corresponds to an LST about 0.35 °C lower (2017) and 0.36 °C lower (2025).

Priority ranking rule. Overlaying the LST and NDVI class layers on the same 1 km grid, each pixel is ranked by two adverse conditions: very high temperature and lack of green cover.

6.1 What is QGIS?

QGIS (Quantum GIS) is a free and open-source Geographic Information System (GIS) software that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. QGIS allows users to display, process, analyze and edit both raster data (satellite imagery) and vector data (administrative boundaries). The software includes a set of processing tools (Processing Toolbox) integrating GDAL, GRASS and SAGA, as well as a map layout editor (Print Layout) for exporting finished maps. Being free and backed by a large community, QGIS is well suited to student teams and agencies that want to reuse workflows without licensing costs.

6.2  Data processing workflow in QGIS

a.     Clipping rasters to the study area boundary. Use the Clip Raster by Mask Layer tool (Raster › Extraction) with the Hanoi boundary vector layer as the mask. Only pixels inside the boundary are kept; pixels outside are set to NoData. This step is applied to LST, NDVI and land cover.

b.     Calculating the mean of raster layers. Use Cell Statistics (Processing Toolbox › Raster analysis) with the Mean statistic and NoData ignored, to combine daily images (LST) or 16-day images (NDVI) into an annual mean image. Each pixel is averaged only over the days that have data. LST is converted to °C using the Raster Calculator: value × 0.02 − 273.15.

c.     Normalizing the data. Use the Raster Calculator with the min–max formula (below), where the minimum and maximum values of each year are taken from the raster layer statistics. The result is a value from 0 to 1.

d.     Classifying the data. Use Reclassify by Table to divide the normalized values into 5 classes: 0–0.2 → 1 (Very Low), 0.2–0.4 → 2 (Low), 0.4–0.6 → 3 (Moderate), 0.6–0.8 → 4 (High), 0.8–1.0 → 5 (Very High). The change layer is created with the Raster Calculator: 2017 class × 10 + 2025 class. For land cover, the Built Area class is extracted separately and the two years are compared to obtain 4 change types.

e.     Calculating area statistics. Use the Raster Layer Unique Values Report to count the number of pixels and the area of each class and each change code; export them to a spreadsheet.

f.      Map layout. Use Print Layout to present finished maps: satellite imagery basemap, coordinate grid, legend, scale bar, north arrow, location map of Vietnam, commune/ward boundaries and water bodies. The maps are exported as high-resolution PNG images and uploaded to the website for download.

6.3 Building the website with Claude and GitHub

The website was built with the support of Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant. Claude wrote the Python scripts that read the rasters and package the data, built the HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface with the Leaflet mapping library, and cross-checked the figures on the website against the original data. The scientific content, methodology and result maps were produced by the team. The source code is stored on GitHub and the website is published publicly for free via GitHub Pages. The website runs entirely in the browser, without its own server; the 10 m built-up land map is cut into small image tiles for fast loading.

6.4 Brand identity

- The UrHeatixel project logo was created with Gemini, featuring the letter H composed of pixel cells and the text URban HEAT monitoring through pIXEL analysis.

- The Long Geo – Geomatics team logo was designed with Canva.

7. Contributions, significance and users

UrHeatixel turns hundreds of scattered satellite images into visual evidence of where it is getting hotter, why, and where intervention is needed first.

7.1  Contributions

- Scientific: quantifies the expansion and direction of spread of high-temperature zones in Hanoi over 2017 – 2025, and links them to built-up land and vegetation cover within a single analytical framework.

- Methodological: a workflow built entirely on free data (NASA MODIS, Esri Sentinel-2) and open-source software (QGIS, Python), easy to repeat for other years or other provinces and cities.

- Product: a public website where values can be viewed down to each pixel and each commune/ward under the new 2025 administrative boundaries, without installing any GIS software.

- Action: a list of hotspots and priority communes/wards, with clear, easy-to-explain ranking rules.

7.2  Significance

- Helps detect early the trend of urbanization spreading to the periphery through land surface temperature signals.

- Provides a basis for allocating urban cooling resources to the right places: according to the results, an NDVI increase of 0.1 corresponds to an LST about 0.35 °C lower.

- Helps raise public awareness of urban heat islands and the role of green cover and water bodies.

7.3 Who uses it and for what

User

Uses UrHeatixel to

City and commune/ward authorities

Identify priority areas for planting trees, building parks and regulating lakes; monitor effectiveness over the years

Planning – architecture and environmental agencies

Include land surface temperature and green cover criteria in planning; limit concrete development in areas that are getting hotter

Researchers and students

Reuse the workflow and data; extend it to other years or other cities

Health and energy sectors

Prioritize heat warnings and forecast electricity demand for hot areas

Residents and communities

Know how hot the area they live in is; take part in greening activities
